Market news Nutrition & Health News USDA details 5-pronged bird flu response plan USDA is investing $1 billion in a comprehensive strategy to curb HPAI, protect the poultry industry and lower egg prices. Kristin Bakker , Digital Content Specialist , Farm Progress Livestock Group February 26, 2025 schedule 5 Min Read USDA has released details of its new $1 billion strategy to combat highly pathogenic avian influenza. U.S. Department of Agriculture Hearing regular pleas from egg, poultry and dairy stakeholders, politicians and consumers for a solution to the ongoing bird flu crisis that’s decimating the nation’s flocks and causing skyrocketing retail egg prices, the U.S. Department of Agriculture has finally released details of its new strategy to combat highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI). Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said USDA will invest $1 billion in a comprehensive strategy to curb HPAI, protect the U.S. poultry industry and lower egg prices to address what she called a “catastrophic” situation. It will include working with the Department of Government Efficiency to identify wasteful spending that could be put toward “investing in long-term solutions to avian flu.” She also noted that the funding is in addition to the indemnity payments already in place to compensate affected producers for depopulating their flocks once they undergo a biosecurity audit. Related: Dairy coalition urges Congress to reject S. 5026 Rollins laid out the strategy at a Feb. 26 meeting of state agriculture department leaders and in an op-ed published in the Wall Street Journal . The prongs of the agency’s five-part plan include: Biosecurity . USDA will invest $500 million into biosecurity to help keep HPAI from entering farms in the first place and preventing its spread. To that end, USDA said it will expand its Wildlife Biosecurity Assessments, beginning with egg-laying facilities, to safeguard farms from wild birds, which cause 83% of HPAI cases. The agency noted that the roughly 150 facilities that follow these protocols have seen only one outbreak. USDA will also expand its free biosecurity audits for all HPAI-affected farms and will share up to 75% of the costs to fix the highest-risk biosecurity issues identified by the assessments and audits. Repopulation . USDA will provide $400 million in financial relief for affected producers this fiscal year. The agency is exploring new programs to help farmers speed up repopulation, including ways to simplify the approval process to speed recovery. Deregulation . In an interview with Fox News, Rollins said, “The egg industry is overregulated; they have too many rules on the books.” USDA said it will work with the Food & Drug Administration to identify potential strategies to safely expand supply in the commercial egg market, in addition to educating Congress and consumers about how regulatory burdens in different regions affect the price of eggs in different markets. USDA also plans to work with farmers and scientists to develop innovative strategies to limit the extent of depopulations in HPAI outbreaks. Related: IRS issues 45Z Clean Fuels Production Tax Credit guidance Research and innovation . USDA will invest up to $100 million for research into possible new animal vaccines, therapeutic tools and other innovative solutions to minimize depopulations – what Rollins called “the longer-term approach.” This will also include increased bio-surveillance and other innovative solutions targeted at egg-laying hens in and around outbreaks. USDA will seek public input on potential solutions while also working with states, veterinarians and poultry and dairy producers on a vaccine and therapeutic strategy, logistics and surveillance. Imports . USDA will explore options for temporarily increasing egg imports – and decreasing exports, if needed – to boost domestic availability, also looking to international best practices in egg production and safety to identify opportunities to increase domestic supply. Vaccine debate The different poultry and egg sectors are divided in their stance on animal vaccination. In testimony during a Senate Agriculture Committee hearing today on “Perspectives from the Field,” United Egg Producers (UEP) board member Tony Wesner of Rose Acre Farms said, “Vaccinations are the only protection we’re going to have.” Pointing to how the HPAI virus has mutated and now affects several animal species and people, he emphasized that a “vaccine needs to be forefront,” but it also needs to be safe and effective. Related: Court allows USDA to proceed with reorganization plan Wesner noted that it could take two to five years to see advancements that result in an improvement, “but we have to do go down this road because it’s the only answer we have. To do nothing is wrong.” National Turkey Federation chairman John Zimmerman testified during the hearing: “We’re beyond biosecurity. We’ve done as much as we can, so we need to look at new tools for our toolbox – and the primary tool we have to look at is vaccination.” Zimmerman added that USDA’s “strategic initiative would help us decide the logistics and the behind-the-doors work that needs to be done to roll out a vaccine strategy for multiple species … to get the viral load diminished in the United States.” The National Chicken Council (NCC), however, has cautioned that vaccinating poultry could have trade implications and emphasized minimizing potential adverse impacts on exports. After the USDA announcement, NCC president Harrison Kircher released a statement applauding the agency’s “commitment to combat HPAI across all species – a common goal shared by U.S. broiler producers. Particularly, we appreciate the measured and science-based approach for the potential use of an effective and applicable vaccine for laying hens and turkeys and the Administration’s commitment to work with our trading partners to minimize any potential negative trade effects should a vaccine ever be used.” He added that NCC intends to work with “the Administration, states, public health professionals and veterinarians to be part of the solution.” The dairy industry has also been significantly affected by HPAI, which doesn’t generally lead to culling of cows but can result in reduced milk production. The National Milk Producers Federation (NMPF) and the International Dairy Foods Association (IDFA) issued a joint statement in response to the USDA avian flu plan. NMPF president and chief executive officer Gregg Doud said, “We support the department’s initiatives to advance vaccine development and deployment that will help control, and ultimately eliminate, the virus in dairy cattle. And we also want to remind consumers that, even as dairy farmers are working with veterinarians and officials at all levels of government to eliminate this animal health threat, milk for consumers remains safe to drink because of the effectiveness of pasteurization.” IDFA president and CEO Dr. Michael Dykes added, “We continue to urge USDA and its federal partners to act quickly to develop and approve the use of safe, effective bovine vaccines to guard against current and future strains of avian influenza affecting U.S. dairy. It is essential that the federal government work with our industry to ensure a vaccination strategy is feasible and cost-effective for farmers while working with international trading partners to assure the use of vaccines does not limit or disrupt U.S. agricultural exports.” About the Author Kristin Bakker Digital Content Specialist, Farm Progress Livestock Group Kristin Bakker contributes content for the Farm Progress Livestock Team, which includes Feedstuffs, BEEF Magazine, and National Hog Farmer. Before this role, she handled content coordination, proofreading, and production duties for Feedstuffs for 25 years.
